*Essence* editor-in-chief Angela Burt-Murray said it took a year for the magazine to gain access to the Obamas’ Illinois home for an intimate interview with the presumptive Democratic presidential nominee; his wife, Michelle; and their daughters, Sasha and Malia.

Burt-Murray spoke Thursday with CNN *American Morning* anchor Kiran Chetry about the interview and the Obama family.

**Chetry:** You are the first African-American media outlet to get this inside look. Did your team get a chance to see the real Obamas?

**Burt-Murray:** I think we did. We went to their home on the South Side of Chicago, and it was wonderful to see them interacting as a family, to see the girls skipping around the house and behaving as though it were a normal, everyday occurrence to have a camera crew in their home and Secret Service agents stationed at various points throughout the house and around the yard. But it did not really seem to affect the girls in any way.

Watch what *Essence* found inside the Obamas’ home »

**Chetry:** Much was made of an earlier televised interview they did with their daughters, and they later said that, looking back, they probably should not have done it. There is so much interest in their family, and yet they want to protect their girls. How do they balance that?

**Burt-Murray:** They try to consider who is around the family and make sure they keep things as structured as possible. But there are also instances where magazines like *Essence* come in to take photographs, and the girls are very relaxed because they are in their home environment. I think that is the difference between our photo shoot and what you saw on television. Taking the girls out of their home and placing them in the spotlight is probably more challenging for them as parents.

**Chetry:** They have to deal with competing stereotypes, if you will: They have been parodied as angry Black radicals and as Ivy League elitists. In the magazine, Gwen Ifill wrote, “The Obamas pride themselves on creating a family picture that is authentically Black with shades of Norman Rockwell.” Explain that. How are they projecting that image?

**Burt-Murray:** I think it reflects the idea that they are simply an average American family. They have strong family values, they are deeply rooted in their community, and they want to give their girls a powerful example of achievement. But they also want to serve as a model for the rest of their community. In our story, the Obamas talk about how important it is for them to continue living in their South Side Chicago neighborhood because it is a neighborhood in transition. Children there have the opportunity to see an African-American man run for the highest office in the nation right in their own neighborhood. So they are modeling not only for their children, but also for the larger community.

**Chetry:** They do live in a gated community, in a $1.6 million home, so that is out of reach for a lot of people.

**Burt-Murray:** But it is also very accessible. While we were there photographing them for *Essence*, you could see cars going by and stopping, with people getting out to take photographs. The girls were on the porch, and people could see them. There is some normalcy there, but it is also obviously something very special and different.

**Chetry:** They said race has been prominent on the campaign trail. Barack Obama told Gwen Ifill that he thinks race is a national obsession. He believes the racial divide is not as significant an issue in this country as it is often made out to be.

**Burt-Murray:** As evidenced by the success he has had with his campaign, you can certainly see that attitudes are shifting. But there are still challenges, obviously, that need to be addressed. It did not appear to affect them much at all.

**Chetry:** There was a lot of attention after a previous television interview that included their daughters, and the Obamas later said they probably should not have done it. People are very interested in their family, but they also want to shield their girls. How do they manage that?

**Burt-Murray:** They seem to be very careful about who is allowed near the family, and they try to keep the girls’ lives as organized and stable as they can. At the same time, there are moments when a publication like Essence comes in to take pictures. Because the girls were at home, they were comfortable and at ease. I think that is what made our photo session different from what happened on television. Bringing the girls out of their own surroundings and placing them directly in the public eye is likely much harder for the Obamas as parents.

**Chetry:** They have had to confront competing stereotypes. Some have portrayed them as angry Black radicals, while others have characterized them as Ivy League elitists. In the magazine, Gwen Ifill wrote that “The Obamas pride themselves on creating a family picture that is authentically black with shades of Norman Rockwell.” What does that mean, and how are they presenting that image?

**Burt-Murray:** I think the point is that they see themselves as a typical American family. They emphasize close family ties, have deep connections to their community and want their daughters to see a strong example of success. They also want to serve as an example for the wider community. In our story, the Obamas discuss why it matters to them to keep living in their South Side Chicago neighborhood, which is undergoing change. **Chetry:** They said race has been a major topic during the campaign. Barack Obama told Gwen Ifill that he believes race is a national fixation. He also said he does not think the racial divide in the United States is as large a problem as it is often portrayed.

Hyde Park is an important part of their story. It’s diverse, intellectual, politically active, and rooted in community life. It helps explain how Barack and Michelle Obama see the world — through education, civic engagement, and neighborhood ties. It also grounds them. They are not presenting themselves as people who came out of nowhere; they have a community, a church history, schools, neighbors, and a real urban American context behind them.

**CHETRY:**  
At the same time, Chicago has also been used by critics to raise questions about associations and politics. How do you think voters are processing that?

**BURT-MURRAY:**  
Voters are hearing a lot of competing narratives. Some people see Chicago as evidence of community organizing and public service. Others hear “Chicago politics” and think of machine politics or controversy. In the Obama campaign, Chicago becomes both an asset and a target. The challenge for the campaign is to keep the focus on his biography — his work, his values, his family — rather than letting opponents define that environment for him.

**CHETRY:**  
Let’s talk about race. Barack Obama has often tried to run a campaign that is not centered solely on race, yet race is obviously part of the conversation. How do you see that balance?

**BURT-MURRAY:**  
It’s a delicate balance. Senator Obama cannot escape the historic nature of being the first Black major-party nominee with a real chance to win the presidency. But he has also made clear that he wants to be judged as a candidate for all Americans. For many Black voters, there is pride, but also anxiety — pride in seeing this moment, and anxiety about how race may be used against him. For white voters, some are inspired by the possibility of turning a page, while others may be confronting biases they don’t always talk about openly.

**CHETRY:**  
Do you think Michelle Obama has faced a different kind of scrutiny because she is a Black woman?

**BURT-MURRAY:**  
Absolutely. Michelle Obama is accomplished, outspoken, and highly educated, and those qualities are often celebrated in political spouses — but with her, they have sometimes been framed negatively. There has been an effort in some quarters to portray her as angry or unpatriotic, and that taps into damaging stereotypes about Black women. At the same time, many women see her as authentic — someone who speaks plainly about marriage, motherhood, career, and the pressures families face.

**CHETRY:**  
How important has *Essence*’s coverage of the Obamas been for your readers?

**BURT-MURRAY:**  
Our readers are deeply engaged in this election. They are interested in policy, certainly — the economy, health care, education, the war — but they are also interested in what this candidacy means culturally and historically. The Obamas’ story resonates because it reflects aspiration, family, partnership, and possibility. For Black women in particular, Michelle Obama’s visibility has been especially meaningful.

**CHETRY:**  
Some critics say the media focuses too much on the “symbolism” of the Obama family and not enough on the issues. Is that a fair criticism?

**BURT-MURRAY:**  
It can be. Symbolism matters, but it should not replace substance. The historic nature of the candidacy is real, and the family image is part of how voters understand candidates. But ultimately, voters also need to hear about jobs, mortgages, schools, health care, and foreign policy. The best coverage connects the personal story to the public stakes without reducing the candidate to biography alone.

**CHETRY:**  
When you look at the Obamas as a family on the campaign trail, what stands out most to you?

**BURT-MURRAY:**  
Their sense of partnership. Michelle Obama is not just standing silently beside her husband; she is an active presence, a validator, and a communicator. And Barack Obama often speaks about his family in ways that feel grounded — the missed dinners, the strain of travel, the importance of his daughters keeping him humble. That makes them relatable, even in the extraordinary circumstances of a presidential campaign.

**CHETRY:**  
And finally, Angela, what do you think this moment means beyond Election Day?

**BURT-MURRAY:**  
Regardless of the outcome, the image of this family has already become part of American political history. It has expanded the public imagination of what a presidential family can look like. It has forced conversations about race, identity, marriage, parenting, and representation. Those conversations will continue long after the campaign is over.

**CHETRY:**  
Angela Burt-Murray, editor-in-chief of *Essence*, thank you so much for joining us.

**BURT-MURRAY:**  
Thank you, Kiran.
